dailyQueue.title: The website never progresses beyond a loading state
dailyQueue.detail: Both supplied screenshots show only a dark burgundy viewport and a small partial-ring loader. No usable interface, fallback message, retry action, or indication of progress is visible.
dailyQueue.evidence: The desktop screenshot at 1500×1000 and mobile screenshot at 780×1656 both contain only the loading indicator. The scan records just 6 visible elements, 3 words, one interactive target, no headings, and no navigation links despite a successful HTTP response and no failed network requests.
dailyQueue.observed: Visitors receive an apparently indefinite loading screen with no way to browse, understand the business, or recover.
dailyQueue.expected: The primary interface should render immediately, with loading restricted to individual dynamic regions. If essential data fails or takes too long, the page should expose branded fallback content, an error state, and a retry or direct-contact route.
dailyQueue.location: Entire page on desktop and mobile
dailyQueue.recommendation: Remove the full-page rendering gate and render the header, value proposition, search controls, contact actions, and cached or skeleton property layout immediately. Add a bounded timeout with an explicit recovery state for any blocking data request.

dailyQueue.title: No premium real-estate proposition is communicated
dailyQueue.detail: Nothing visible identifies Inmobiliaria Noguera, its premium positioning, or its Écija and Sevilla market. The visitor cannot determine what business the page belongs to.
dailyQueue.evidence: There is no visible logo, agency name, headline, supporting copy, location, or property content in either screenshot. The DOM has no H1 and a total word count of 3.
dailyQueue.observed: The first viewport is an anonymous loading screen.
dailyQueue.expected: A reference-quality premium agency should establish its name, market, offer, and point of distinction immediately through confident typography, strong property imagery, and concise location-specific messaging.
dailyQueue.location: First viewport on desktop and mobile
dailyQueue.recommendation: Make the agency name a prominent first-viewport signal and add a clear Spanish H1 describing the offer and geography, supported by a concise differentiator such as local expertise, curated homes, or discreet advisory service.

dailyQueue.title: There is no visible property inventory or discovery path
dailyQueue.detail: The secondary business goal cannot be completed because visitors cannot see listings, search, filters, categories, or navigation to properties.
dailyQueue.evidence: The scan reports 0 images, 0 navigation links, 0 headings, and only one interactive target. Neither screenshot contains property cards, search controls, filters, map access, or inventory categories.
dailyQueue.observed: There is no route into the available property portfolio.
dailyQueue.expected: Premium real-estate browsing should expose representative listings quickly and support filtering by location, property type, operation, price, bedrooms, and other market-relevant criteria.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Render a prominent property search and a curated initial selection above or immediately below the fold. Provide concise filters and clear links into complete sales, rental, and featured-property inventories.

dailyQueue.title: The primary enquiry journey is absent
dailyQueue.detail: A prospective buyer or seller cannot contact the agency or enquire about a property from the rendered page.
dailyQueue.evidence: The DOM contains no primary CTA, no contact signals, no booking signals, and no forms. The screenshots show no phone, WhatsApp, email, consultation CTA, or property-enquiry action.
dailyQueue.observed: The page offers zero visible conversion routes despite property enquiry being the primary goal.
dailyQueue.expected: Persistent but restrained contact access should be available from the first viewport, with property-specific enquiry actions on listings and detail pages. Mobile should make calling or WhatsApp particularly efficient.
dailyQueue.location: Global header, first viewport, property browsing, and mobile interface
dailyQueue.recommendation: Add a clear primary action such as “Solicitar información,” plus phone and WhatsApp access. Carry the selected property reference into a short enquiry form and provide a visible response-time or service expectation.

dailyQueue.title: There is effectively no customer-facing content
dailyQueue.detail: The page provides no inventory descriptions, service information, market guidance, agency story, or explanation of what happens after an enquiry.
dailyQueue.evidence: The scan measures only 3 words, no heading samples, no images, and no visible content sections.
dailyQueue.observed: Visitors have no information with which to assess relevance, quality, or next steps.
dailyQueue.expected: The site should concisely cover featured properties, buying and selling services, locations served, local market knowledge, and the enquiry process, with fuller detail available deeper in the journey.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Create a focused Spanish content hierarchy led by the property portfolio, followed by service and location expertise. Use specific claims and useful details rather than generic luxury language.

issues.detail: The primary reservation journey stops at an availability enquiry. The page has a date/vehicle form and multiple reservation-oriented CTAs, but the scan reports `bookingSignalCount: 0`; the visible form only promises that dates and final terms will be confirmed directly by Mfinity. A reference-quality luxury rental site should make the next step, response expectation, and reservation mechanism explicit. Connect the availability action to a clear enquiry or booking flow, state what happens after submission, provide response timing, and distinguish an actual reservation from a lead request.
issues.evidence: Hero form is labeled `CHECK AVAILABILITY`; supporting copy says `Dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity`; objective scan reports `bookingSignalCount: 0` despite `primaryCtaCount: 4`.
issues.expected: A decisive, transparent booking path with confirmation state, required information, response expectations, and a clear distinction between availability check, enquiry, and confirmed reservation.
issues.location: Hero availability form and adjacent `RESERVE NOW` CTAs
issues.observed: The interface looks like a booking tool, but operationally behaves like an unqualified enquiry form.
issues.recommendation: Define the post-submit workflow and expose it in the UI. Use a CTA such as `REQUEST THIS CAR` or implement an actual reservation step, then show confirmation, contact method, response time, and what is still subject to approval.
issues.title: The apparent booking flow does not complete a booking

issues.detail: Vehicle discovery is visually dominated by atmosphere rather than product inspection. The desktop hero uses a heavily blurred background and the mobile crop leaves only a partial car visible behind the form. For luxury rental, the vehicle itself is the commercial product and should be immediately inspectable, especially on mobile. Replace or supplement the abstract hero crop with sharp, well-lit vehicle photography and ensure the first meaningful collection cards show model, specification, price basis, and availability.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots show a strongly defocused background; on mobile the Ferrari is largely obscured by the oversized headline and availability panel. The business requirements explicitly include vehicle photography and mobile vehicle discovery.
issues.expected: Cinematic imagery can remain part of the brand, but the vehicle silhouette, model, finish, and condition should be clearly legible in the first viewport and throughout discovery.
issues.location: Hero background and initial mobile viewport
issues.observed: The opening experience communicates mood more strongly than the actual rental inventory.
issues.recommendation: Use a crisp hero image with deliberate car positioning, reduce the overlay/form obstruction, and bring a compact, swipeable vehicle discovery row or clearly visible collection preview into the mobile first viewport.
issues.title: The hero sells ambience before it sells the cars

issues.detail: Pricing clarity is insufficient for a high-intent rental audience. The featured panel exposes `From €1,400 / day` for one Ferrari and mentions a deposit, but the rest of the fleet appears to rely on discovery before users can compare costs or rental conditions. The benchmark specifically requires pricing clarity. Reference execution should make the pricing model and major qualification variables easy to compare without forcing a lead first.
issues.evidence: The hero only shows `From €1,400 / day` for the featured Ferrari, with `Deposit €7,000 · longer rentals on request`; no broader pricing or rental-condition summary is visible in either screenshot.
issues.expected: Users can quickly compare indicative daily rates, deposit requirements, included mileage, insurance, delivery, and longer-rental rules across relevant vehicles.
issues.location: Hero featured-vehicle panel and collection entry point
issues.observed: There is one price anchor, but not enough commercial information to support vehicle selection or qualified enquiry.
issues.recommendation: Add indicative rate/deposit data to vehicle cards or detail pages, include a concise `what's included` summary, and make date-dependent pricing behavior explicit.
issues.title: Pricing does not support comparison or qualification

issues.detail: The page gives no visible trust proof despite selling a high-value transaction. The objective scan reports `trustSignalCount: 0`, and the screenshots show no testimonials, review rating, fleet-care proof, rental credentials, insurance explanation, delivery process, or customer reassurance beyond the phrase `regular inspections & maintenance`. Luxury customers need confidence in both the cars and the operator before submitting personal dates and contact details.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports `trustSignalCount: 0`; visible copy is limited to `regular inspections & maintenance` and `direct local contact`, with no review, policy, company, or service proof in the captured page.
issues.expected: Specific, verifiable reassurance placed near the booking action: local operating details, review evidence, insurance/deposit clarity, fleet preparation standards, delivery coverage, and clear terms.
issues.location: Hero reassurance copy, booking form, and below-fold experience section
issues.observed: The brand asserts premium service but provides little evidence that reduces perceived booking risk.
issues.recommendation: Add concise trust modules adjacent to the form and vehicle details, backed by real evidence: verified reviews, local address/contact, fleet-care protocol, insurance/deposit terms, and transparent rental policies.
issues.title: Premium positioning is under-supported by trust evidence

issues.detail: The mobile first viewport is overloaded. The large three-line headline, long supporting paragraph, form, availability disclaimer, service reassurance, and two large action buttons are all stacked over the same image. This makes the core choice and the next action compete for attention, while the lower `VEHICLE CARE` and `FLEET STANDARD` content is visibly entering the viewport without enough separation. A reference-quality mobile funnel would prioritize one decision at a time and preserve a clean transition into vehicle discovery.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot shows the hero copy occupying most of the upper screen, followed by a tall form, two explanatory text blocks, two large buttons, and the next section title visible at the bottom. The form itself expands from two date fields into a full-width vehicle selector and CTA.
issues.expected: A controlled mobile hierarchy: concise promise, one primary action or compact availability form, clear reassurance, then an intentional handoff to the fleet.
issues.location: Mobile hero from headline through the start of the next section
issues.observed: Everything is technically contained, but the first screen asks the user to absorb too much before discovering vehicles.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the supporting copy, collapse secondary reassurance into a compact line, make the booking action primary, and move service-positioning content below the first vehicle discovery block.
issues.title: Mobile hierarchy is too dense for the booking moment

issues.detail: The typography and controls lean toward a generic editorial landing-page treatment rather than precise luxury commerce. The very large geometric headline, widely tracked uppercase labels, outlined `CONTROL` button, and all-caps navigation create a stylized template impression. The scan also identifies five font families and an inconsistent button ratio of `0.3333`, which is consistent with the visible mix of outlined, text, dark, and white button treatments. A high-end rental interface should have a tighter type system and a more deliberate action hierarchy.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot shows several button styles and widely tracked micro-labels; mobile screenshot uses an unusually oversized headline relative to the transactional form. Objective scan reports `fontFamilyCount: 5` and `inconsistentButtonRatio: 0.3333333333333333`.
issues.expected: A restrained type scale with one display face and one supporting interface face, consistent control geometry, and a clearly dominant reservation action.
issues.location: Global header, hero typography, availability form, and primary CTAs
issues.observed: The design is polished at a glance but feels more like a branded concept page than a mature rental product.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the display scale on mobile, normalize font roles and letter spacing, remove or rename ambiguous controls such as `CONTROL`, and establish one primary button treatment with a restrained secondary style.
issues.title: The visual system feels stylized but not fully resolved

issues.detail: The language is evocative but not sufficiently concrete for a location-specific rental decision. `Luxury in every kilometer` and `Keep the feeling` communicate aspiration, while the useful operational details are relegated to small supporting text. Marbella and Puerto Banús customers also need immediate clarity around delivery area, pickup, airport/hotel delivery, driver age or license requirements, and rental terms.
issues.evidence: Hero copy is primarily emotional: `Luxury in every kilometer`, `A collection built for Marbella at full volume`, and `Choose the car. Keep the feeling`. The visible location statement only says Marbella and Costa del Sol; no Puerto Banús service or delivery terms are shown.
issues.expected: Brand language paired with concise, specific service facts that qualify the audience and reduce friction at the point of enquiry.
issues.location: Hero copy and first booking interaction
issues.observed: The site establishes mood and geography, but does not quickly explain the practical service promise.
issues.recommendation: Keep the tone, then add compact operational proof near the form: Marbella/Puerto Banús delivery coverage, pickup options, minimum rental period, deposit/insurance headline terms, and expected response time.
issues.title: The promise is more poetic than operational

issues.detail: The CTA set contains competing labels and destinations. The header says `RENT ONLINE`, the hero says `CHECK AVAILABILITY`, the featured card says `RESERVE NOW`, and mobile presents `WHATSAPP` beside `RENT A CAR`. With no visible indication of how these routes differ, users may hesitate or choose a lower-commitment channel when the business goal is a qualified reservation.
issues.evidence: The screenshots visibly show four different reservation/contact labels across header, hero card, form, and mobile action row; the scan reports four primary CTAs and two contact signals.
issues.expected: One dominant conversion route supported by a clearly secondary WhatsApp/contact option, with labels that describe the actual outcome of each action.
issues.location: Global header, hero card, availability form, and mobile action row
issues.observed: The interface offers many plausible next steps without a single unambiguous conversion hierarchy.
issues.recommendation: Choose one primary action, use the same wording consistently, and label WhatsApp as a fast contact alternative with a clear purpose and expected response.
issues.title: Multiple reservation CTAs dilute the conversion hierarchy

aiReview.summary: Mfinity has a strong visual premise and an unusually solid technical baseline, but it currently behaves more like a cinematic brand introduction than a reference-quality luxury rental funnel. The largest commercial gaps are the incomplete booking path, weak trust proof, limited pricing transparency, and imagery that obscures rather than showcases the fleet. Desktop feels polished; mobile is functional but overpacked and places too much content over the hero. The site is above average and likely capable of generating enquiries, but the supplied experience does not yet justify the 90+ range for a business whose critical journey is booking.
strengths: The page establishes a recognizable Marbella luxury mood immediately and uses a relevant Ferrari hero asset rather than generic imagery.
The core business proposition is clear: premium and performance vehicles for Marbella and the Costa del Sol.
The availability form is visible in the hero, includes dates and vehicle selection, and adapts to a usable mobile stack.
The visual execution has strong contrast, a restrained black-and-white base, cinematic composition, and no obvious accessibility or performance defects in the supplied measurements.
The scan confirms a sound technical foundation: fast loading, no horizontal overflow, valid internal links, labeled controls, complete image alt coverage, and strong SEO/geographic basics.

issues.detail: The primary lead journey asks visitors to start a project but provides no visible low-friction way to enquire, estimate scope, or contact the business from the homepage.
issues.evidence: The scan finds 0 forms, 0 contact signals, 0 booking signals, and only 2 primary CTAs. Neither screenshot shows a phone number, email address, WhatsApp action, enquiry fields, or response-time expectation.
issues.expected: A reference-quality specialist services site should let qualified buyers initiate contact immediately and should explain what happens after submission. It should support both high-intent visitors ready for a quote and earlier-stage visitors who still need guidance.
issues.location: Homepage header, hero and lead-enquiry journey
issues.observed: “Solicitar presupuesto” and “Cuéntanos tu proyecto” are generic links that send the visitor elsewhere before collecting any useful information. Mobile users also lose the header quote CTA behind the menu.
issues.recommendation: Add a short homepage enquiry module with project type, location, date or operating period, capacity, and contact details. Keep phone and WhatsApp or email visibly available, especially on mobile. State an honest response-time commitment and make the next step explicit.
issues.title: The lead journey lacks immediate contact and capture

issues.detail: The site makes several commercial claims but presents no evidence that reduces the perceived risk of hiring a specialist transport operator or supplier.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 0 trust signals. The supplied hero screenshots contain no client names, project figures, certifications, safety credentials, years of experience, geographic coverage, testimonials, or recognizable deployments.
issues.expected: Professional transport services should substantiate credibility with real projects, named clients where permitted, operating history, fleet or passenger figures, safety and compliance information, and specific outcomes.
issues.location: Homepage, particularly immediately after the hero and before the final enquiry point
issues.observed: The presentation looks polished, but visitors are asked to trust the company based primarily on tone and a single vehicle image. This leaves municipalities, event organizers, and venue operators without procurement-grade reassurance.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a compact proof band near the top with verified operating figures and credentials, followed by two or three case studies showing client or place, challenge, supplied service, capacity, duration, and outcome. Use authentic deployment photography and link every claim to supporting detail.
issues.title: There is no visible proof behind the specialist positioning

issues.detail: The core proposition combines manufacturing, rental, and sales for multiple audiences without helping visitors identify the correct service or commercial model quickly.
issues.evidence: The hero copy reads “Fabricación, alquiler y venta para ciudades, eventos y espacios…”. The heading samples later divide the offer into “Ciudades y turismo”, “Ferias y celebraciones”, and “Empresas y espacios”, while the site contains additional pages for municipalities, events, weddings, Christmas floats, and parades.
issues.expected: A strong B2B homepage should distinguish what can be hired, purchased, manufactured, or managed; who each option is for; and the main qualification criteria for each route.
issues.location: Hero proposition and service overview
issues.observed: The breadth of the offer is visible, but the service architecture is audience-led in some places and product-led in others. A buyer cannot immediately determine whether the company supplies vehicles only, operates routes, handles staffing and permits, or offers an end-to-end service.
issues.recommendation: Reframe the offer into three explicit commercial paths such as operation and management, vehicle rental, and manufacture or purchase. For each, state the target buyer, included scope, typical use cases, service area, and a dedicated enquiry action.
issues.title: Service breadth is not translated into purchasing clarity

issues.detail: The calls to action do not set expectations or help visitors self-qualify before making contact.
issues.evidence: Visible CTAs use “Solicitar presupuesto”, “Cuéntanos tu proyecto”, and “Conocer los vehículos”. The scan records a 27.27% inconsistent button ratio and no booking or contact signals.
issues.expected: Conversion copy should match visitor intent and disclose what information is required, whether the service is available in the visitor’s location, and what the response will contain.
issues.location: Desktop header, hero buttons and downstream text actions
issues.observed: The two lead CTAs express slightly different intentions without clarifying whether they reach the same destination. Secondary links use several visual and verbal patterns, which weakens the sense of one deliberate funnel.
issues.recommendation: Choose one primary enquiry label and use it consistently. Pair it with qualifying microcopy such as “Cuéntanos ciudad, fecha y capacidad” and a clear response expectation. Reserve “Ver vehículos” and “Ver casos” for distinct discovery journeys.
issues.title: CTA language and hierarchy are not fully coherent

issues.detail: The mobile hero consumes substantially more than the first viewport, delaying service explanation, proof, and portfolio discovery.
issues.evidence: In the 780 × 1688 mobile screenshot, the hero occupies nearly the entire captured page and ends around the bottom edge. The oversized heading spans approximately six lines, followed by a long paragraph and two full-width buttons; no following section is meaningfully visible.
issues.expected: The mobile first view should establish the offer, show a decisive action, and leave a visible cue to the next substantive section. Display typography should remain forceful without turning the whole first screen into a poster.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero
issues.observed: The composition is visually dramatic, but the heading and vertical spacing create a long scroll before users can see services or evidence. The second CTA adds further height while competing with the primary action.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the mobile heading size and line count, tighten the gap below the header, shorten the supporting copy, and reduce button stack spacing. Let the next service or proof band enter the initial viewport. Keep the secondary vehicle action visually quieter or move it just below the hero.
issues.title: The mobile hero delays the information buyers need next

issues.detail: A large share of interactive elements are too small for comfortable repeated use, particularly navigation and downstream text links.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies 20 tiny targets among 33 interactive targets, a 53.57% ratio. Desktop navigation links are measured at only 18px high with 12.5px text; several text actions are 17–20.4px high. The small header quote button uses 11px text and is 39px high.
issues.expected: Primary navigation and all actionable links should have reliable touch or pointer hit areas, generally around 44px high on mobile, while retaining clear focus and hover states.
issues.location: Desktop navigation, mobile menu, header CTA and content text links
issues.observed: The large hero buttons are usable, but the broader interaction system relies on small type and narrow hit boxes. This creates a mismatch between the confident visual presentation and the precision required to navigate it.
issues.recommendation: Increase navigation and text-link hit areas with padding without necessarily enlarging every visual label. Bring functional text to at least 14–16px where space allows and ensure every mobile menu item has a full-width 44px or larger row.
issues.title: More than half of the interactive targets are undersized

issues.detail: The hero image is relevant but does not present the service with the clarity and finish expected of a premium specialist operator.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots use one darkened frame dominated by a close crop of a red train. On desktop, a partially visible person occupies the lower-left foreground; on mobile, the train is cropped into body panels and a wheel while much of the vehicle and operating context disappear. The site has only 4 images in total.
issues.expected: Reference-quality imagery should clearly show the complete product, passengers or staff where relevant, the destination context, and authentic real-world operation. Crops should remain intentional at every breakpoint.
issues.location: Homepage hero and overall image system
issues.observed: The image proves that a vehicle exists, but it does not clearly communicate scale, passenger experience, route environment, fleet quality, or service delivery. The heavy dark overlay further suppresses useful vehicle detail.
issues.recommendation: Commission or select a wider, sharper hero photograph showing the complete train in operation in a recognizable Spanish setting. Art-direct separate mobile and desktop crops. Build a supporting image set covering interiors, accessibility, passengers, events, team operations, and multiple vehicle types.
issues.title: The imagery is authentic but insufficiently informative

issues.detail: The absence of visible legal and privacy routes weakens confidence at the exact point where personal and project data would be submitted.
issues.evidence: The scan finds no privacy link and no legal link. It also records a security and trust score of 75.4 and no visible trust signals.
issues.expected: A Spanish professional services site seeking leads should provide readily discoverable legal notice, privacy information, company identity, and relevant data-processing disclosures in the footer and beside any enquiry form.
issues.location: Global footer and future enquiry form
issues.observed: Visitors cannot readily verify the legal entity or understand how enquiry data will be handled. This is especially conspicuous for municipal and corporate buyers performing supplier checks.
issues.recommendation: Add complete “Aviso legal” and “Política de privacidad” pages, identify the contracting entity and business address, and link the relevant privacy disclosure directly from the enquiry form.
issues.title: Essential legal and company trust information is missing

issues.detail: The type system alternates between oversized display text and very small functional labels, reducing consistency and legibility.
issues.evidence: The scan finds 4 font families and 26 tiny text elements, representing 14.2% of visible elements. Examples include 9px brand and vehicle labels, 10px overlines, 11px tags and CTA text, and 12–12.5px navigation and action links. The mobile H1 is exceptionally large by comparison.
issues.expected: A mature identity should have a controlled type scale with a readable functional floor, consistent roles, and fewer family changes. Expressiveness should not depend on extreme contrast between poster-size headlines and miniature labels.
issues.location: Header branding, navigation, hero, overlines, tags and vehicle sections
issues.observed: The sans-serif and italic serif pairing gives the hero distinction, but repeated uppercase micro-labels and very small actions feel editorial rather than operational. Some supporting information becomes visually subordinate beyond its actual importance.
issues.recommendation: Consolidate the typography into two families with explicit display, heading, body, label, and action tokens. Set a 14px minimum for meaningful interface text, reserve 10–12px only for nonessential metadata, and reduce the mobile display scale to restore a more balanced hierarchy.
issues.title: Typography is expressive but operational text is too small

issues.detail: The homepage is too concise for the complexity and procurement risk of the offer.
issues.evidence: The scan records only 396 words across a business offering manufacturing, rental, sales, event use, municipal service, vehicles, and management. Heading samples emphasize broad benefits and audience categories rather than process, inclusions, requirements, or outcomes.
issues.expected: A specialist services homepage should answer scope, coverage, capacities, accessibility, staffing, logistics, setup, maintenance, compliance, timelines, and the route from enquiry to delivery, while linking to deeper detail.
issues.location: Homepage service, vehicle and company content
issues.observed: The copy is concise and brand-led, but much of the practical information needed to form a qualified lead is deferred. This risks attracting vague enquiries while losing buyers who need to verify fit before contacting a supplier.
issues.recommendation: Add concise but concrete sections for service scope, vehicle capacities and configurations, geographic coverage, project process, common buyer questions, and operational responsibilities. Use tables or scannable specification lists where comparison matters.
issues.title: Content depth does not match the complexity of the service

issues.detail: Local relevance is signaled through Écija and Sevilla, but the operating footprint for the wider Spanish market is unclear.
issues.evidence: The scan shows “DESDE ÉCIJA · SEVILLA” and an Écija case link, while the business market is Spain. The hero says the service is for cities, events, and spaces but gives no visible coverage area.
issues.expected: Visitors should immediately understand whether the company operates locally, across Andalucía, throughout mainland Spain, or in selected regions, including any transport or deployment constraints.
issues.location: Hero supporting copy, proof strip and enquiry qualification
issues.observed: The local origin adds authenticity, but it may also make national buyers uncertain about availability. No visible line resolves whether vehicles and operating teams travel beyond the home region.
issues.recommendation: State the real service footprint near the primary CTA and repeat it in the enquiry flow. Add regional project examples or a deployment map only where those claims can be substantiated.

issues.detail: One of the limited media assets lacks alternative text, and the generally small text system may make supporting information difficult to perceive.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 25% of images missing alt text, specifically the YouTube thumbnail, alongside 26 tiny text elements and an accessibility score of 85.74.
issues.expected: Meaningful project or vehicle media should have context-appropriate alternative text, while decorative media should be explicitly ignored. Supporting copy and controls should remain readable without relying on visual scale extremes.
issues.location: Embedded video or media section and small labels throughout the homepage
issues.observed: The media item is not fully described to nonvisual users, and small labels carry categories and actions that may be important for orientation.
issues.recommendation: Give the video thumbnail or iframe an accessible title describing the route or project shown. Audit all image purposes, correct alt handling, and increase the size and contrast of meaningful labels and actions.
issues.title: Media description and small-text accessibility need refinement

topPriority.title: No detectable enquiry/contact path

aiReview.summary: Trenes y Tranvías has a distinctive, fast, and visually confident foundation, but it currently behaves more like a polished brand introduction than a mature lead-generation site for a specialist transport supplier. The strongest assets are the immediate product signal, memorable headline, disciplined palette, and excellent technical delivery. The main commercial weaknesses are more consequential: no visible contact method or lead capture, no substantiated proof, unclear service and geographic scope, and insufficient procurement-level detail. Mobile presentation remains dramatic but spends too much vertical space on the hero, while the wider interface contains many undersized targets and labels. Raising the site into the high-80s would require stronger proof, clearer service architecture, explicit operating coverage, a properly designed enquiry flow, better art-directed photography, and a more controlled functional type scale.
strengths: The hero establishes the actual product immediately with relevant, authentic-looking train imagery rather than generic tourism photography.
The black, white, red, and yellow palette is distinctive and appropriate to a transport identity; the serif emphasis in “a bordo” gives the brand more character than a typical services template.
The primary headline is direct, memorable, and visually dominant, while the supporting line identifies manufacturing, rental, sales, and key audience contexts.
Desktop and mobile layouts show stable composition with no horizontal overflow or visible layout shift; measured CLS is effectively zero.
Performance is excellent: 476ms desktop LCP, 608ms mobile LCP, 11ms desktop blocking time, and only 163KB transferred.
The document structure is sound, with one H1, orderly heading levels, unique headings, valid internal links, and no console or network errors.
Portfolio discovery has a useful foundation through dedicated pages for vehicles, solutions, management, municipalities, events, weddings, Christmas floats, parades, and the Écija case.
The mobile primary CTA is large, high-contrast, and easy to identify, and the header reduces to a conventional menu without visible overflow.

issues.detail: The mobile hero is not composed for the viewport. The headline and supporting copy sit over a busy marina image with insufficient separation, and the copy becomes difficult to read. The “Marbella, from the water.” headline is visibly crowded against the lower image area, while the paragraph runs across multiple lines with weak contrast.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot: the H1 overlaps the marina, rigging and rooftops; the paragraph spans five lines across the image and competes with the background. Objective scan also reports 62 tiny-text elements and a 28.8% tiny-text ratio.
issues.expected: Reference-quality mobile art direction should preserve a clear reading zone for the value proposition, use a controlled crop or alternate image, and maintain deliberate contrast without forcing text over visually noisy details.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero
issues.observed: The first-viewport message feels visually compromised and harder to scan than the desktop version.
issues.recommendation: Use a mobile-specific focal crop or calmer yacht image, establish a stronger readable overlay, reduce the supporting copy to one concise proposition, and size the hero around the actual mobile composition rather than shrinking the desktop treatment.
issues.title: Mobile hero readability and composition break down

issues.detail: The primary enquiry control is effectively pushed below the useful mobile first viewport. The desktop charter selector is a horizontal strip, but on mobile it becomes a very tall vertical panel that consumes the screen without exposing the final action.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot shows the Guests, Duration, Departure and The Day fields stacked vertically from approximately mid-screen to the bottom, with “Find My Charter” absent from the captured first viewport. Desktop shows the CTA clearly at the right edge of the selector.
issues.expected: The critical charter journey should expose a clear enquiry action immediately on mobile, with compact fields, progressive disclosure, or a persistent bottom CTA.
issues.location: Homepage charter selector below the hero
issues.observed: A mobile visitor can see the inputs but not the conversion action without a long scroll.
issues.recommendation: Recompose the selector for mobile into a compact summary plus one prominent enquiry button, or make the CTA sticky and visible while the fields remain open.
issues.title: Mobile conversion action is below the fold

issues.detail: The site presents a premium charter proposition but gives visitors almost no trust evidence before asking them to enquire. The experience relies on atmosphere and local-experience copy without visible proof of operational credibility.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports trustSignalCount: 0. The supplied homepage screenshots show no reviews, verified credentials, captain or crew information, insurance/safety reassurance, booking process, or partner affiliations.
issues.expected: A luxury charter reference site should make risk-reducing proof visible near the first enquiry path: years operating locally, verified testimonials, vessel standards, crew credentials, response expectations, and clear booking safeguards.
issues.location: Homepage hero and initial conversion section
issues.observed: The €4,375-plus purchase context is not supported by enough visible evidence to justify confidence in the operator.
issues.recommendation: Add concise, specific trust proof adjacent to the enquiry path and fleet content. Use real testimonials and identifiable operational details rather than generic claims such as “more than fifteen years of local experience.”
issues.title: Premium pricing lacks visible trust support

issues.detail: The first visual signal is a marina and apartment backdrop rather than the charter product. Visitors immediately see Puerto Banús scenery and docked boats, but not the specific yachts, onboard experience, crew, or luxury service they are being asked to purchase.
issues.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots are dominated by the same marina image; the yachts are partially obscured by the overlay and surrounding vessels. The homepage has only 2 images despite fleet discovery being a stated business requirement.
issues.expected: The first viewport should make the actual charter offer unmistakable: a well-photographed hero yacht or an onboard moment, followed by clear access to fleet, experience, and destination choices.
issues.location: Homepage first viewport
issues.observed: The setting communicates location, but the product and service differentiation are delayed.
issues.recommendation: Lead with a high-quality image of the actual flagship vessel or a real guest experience, retain the Marbella location cue as supporting context, and make the fleet/enquiry path visually immediate.
issues.title: The product is less prominent than the destination backdrop

issues.detail: The copy is evocative but under-informative for a purchase decision. The opening promise describes a feeling and mentions sailing, fishing and group experiences, yet it does not quickly clarify charter types, starting price context, inclusions, availability handling, or what makes this operator different.
issues.evidence: The visible hero copy is “Private yacht charter, sailing, fishing and group experiences shaped around the people on board” plus “more than fifteen years of local experience.” The scan reports 551 words and no trust signals.
issues.expected: Luxury positioning can remain elegant while answering practical high-intent questions: who the charter is for, what is included, typical duration, approximate price range, departure points, and how quickly an enquiry is handled.
issues.location: Homepage hero and opening content sections
issues.observed: The tone is aspirational, but the visitor must explore several pages before understanding the commercial offer.
issues.recommendation: Add compact, editorially styled commercial context near the first CTA: charter formats, indicative starting prices or price bands, inclusions, capacity, departure area, and a specific enquiry response promise.
issues.title: Atmosphere outweighs decision-making information

issues.detail: The visual language is polished at a glance but still reads close to a luxury-travel template: oversized editorial serif headline, uppercase tracking, muted dark overlay, cream information strip, and sparse navigation. The design does not yet establish a distinctive Marbella or Puerto Banús signature.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot shows a familiar full-bleed marina hero with a centered editorial headline and a dark/cream split CTA strip. Objective scan reports only 2 images, 4 font families, and 33 colors, suggesting a thin asset system with several typographic variables.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution should have a recognizable art direction tied to the actual fleet, coastline, service style, and destination, with a controlled typographic system and imagery that feels owned rather than interchangeable.
issues.location: Homepage visual system, especially hero and opening selector
issues.observed: The page feels competent and premium-adjacent, but not exclusive or memorable enough for a high-value charter brand.
issues.recommendation: Build a tighter art direction around the real boats, onboard service, and Costa del Sol coastline. Reduce font-family variation, define clearer type roles, and use a more distinctive image sequence rather than relying on one marina scene.
issues.title: Premium aesthetic remains too template-adjacent

issues.detail: The interaction targets and labels are too small for a premium mobile booking workflow. The navigation and supporting links are visually delicate, and the desktop phone number is particularly easy to miss or tap inaccurately.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports tinyTapTargetRatio: 0.5 across 43 interactive targets, with 25 tiny targets. Samples include 12.5px navigation links, an 11.5px phone link, and 10.4px text links.
issues.expected: Mobile controls should provide comfortable touch areas, clear active states, and readable labels while preserving the restrained visual style.
issues.location: Global header, navigation, and homepage text links
issues.observed: The interface favors visual quietness over reliable repeated use, especially for visitors trying to call or navigate on a phone.
issues.recommendation: Increase hit areas to practical touch dimensions, give the phone action an icon and stronger prominence, and retain the small uppercase styling only as a visual treatment around a larger interactive area.
issues.title: Delicate controls reduce mobile usability

issues.detail: The fleet content exposes only a small selection on the homepage, and the visible pricing context is not developed into a useful comparison framework. For a charter buyer, vessel choice, capacity, size, location and price are central to the decision.
issues.evidence: The scan lists three homepage yacht headings and one visible price sample in the tiny-text evidence: “From €4,375,” “21.70 m · 12 guests,” and “Puerto Banús.” The business requirement explicitly includes fleet discovery and pricing context.
issues.expected: Fleet discovery should support quick comparison with consistent photography, capacity, length, charter type, price basis, and direct enquiry actions for every vessel.
issues.location: Homepage private selection and fleet journey
issues.observed: The information is present in fragments but does not yet feel like a confident selection tool for a high-value purchase.
issues.recommendation: Standardize each vessel card and detail page around comparable commercial facts, clarify whether pricing is per half-day, full day, or starting rate, and attach an enquiry action to each yacht.
issues.title: Fleet discovery lacks enough comparison depth

issues.detail: The header provides a generic “Plan a charter” action, while the hero uses “Find My Charter,” and the surrounding links use “View the full fleet” and “Explore...” labels. The actions are related but do not establish one consistently dominant enquiry path.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot shows “Plan a charter” in the header and “Find My Charter” in the selector. Objective scan reports 4 primary CTAs and an inconsistentButtonRatio of 0.2093.
issues.expected: A high-converting charter site should use one primary action vocabulary and a clear hierarchy: enquire or check availability as the dominant action, with fleet and inspiration as secondary routes.
issues.location: Header, hero selector, and homepage section links
issues.observed: The user has several plausible next actions without a strong distinction between booking intent and discovery intent.
issues.recommendation: Choose one primary label such as “Enquire about a charter” or “Check availability,” repeat it consistently, and visually subordinate fleet, experience, and destination exploration links.
issues.title: CTA hierarchy and language are not fully unified

issues.detail: One navigational destination is broken, which undermines confidence in a relatively small, high-intent site. “About” is presented as a normal route but does not resolve successfully.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports brokenInternalLinkRatio: 0.0833 and specifically identifies `https://marbellaboatcharter.vercel.app/about.html` as broken.
issues.expected: Every visible navigation route should resolve to a complete page or be removed until it is ready.
issues.location: Global navigation, About route
issues.observed: A visitor following the brand-story path encounters a dead end during a trust-building journey.
issues.recommendation: Repair the About destination or remove the link and route the story content to an existing working page.
issues.title: About navigation route is broken

aiReview.summary: Marbella Boat Charter has a credible geographic premise, a polished desktop first impression, and strong underlying performance and crawlability. The experience falls short of reference-quality luxury charter work because the product is visually secondary to the marina backdrop, the commercial and trust case is thin, and the mobile hero and enquiry flow are materially weaker than desktop. The highest-priority work is to make the actual fleet and service feel tangible, expose trust and pricing context near the enquiry path, and redesign the mobile conversion composition so the CTA is immediately usable.
strengths: The homepage establishes Marbella, Puerto Banús and Costa del Sol immediately, which is relevant geographic positioning for the niche.
The desktop hero has a coherent editorial composition, strong contrast between the image and cream selector strip, and a clear initial charter action.
The charter selector communicates useful intent variables: guests, duration, departure and type of day.
The site appears fast and technically stable according to the supplied measurements: 1,004ms LCP, 0.0006 CLS, no console errors, no failed requests, and no horizontal overflow in the automated check.
The information architecture supports fleet, experiences, destinations, owners, contact and booking journeys, while the page structure and image alt coverage are sound.

issues.title: Mobile hero hierarchy collapses into overlapping, low-legibility content
issues.detail: On the mobile capture, several separate identity and messaging layers compete in the same visual field: the large MARBELLA FOR SALE masthead, the all-caps advisory line, a much larger but extremely low-contrast “Marbella, chosen well.” H1, body copy, and the two CTAs. The H1 appears partially obscured/ghosted against the pool image and sits behind the advisory line rather than leading the reading order.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot visibly shows the oversized faint H1 overlapping the advisory line and image detail. The scan confirms the page H1 is “Marbella, chosen well.” while the branded FOR SALE text is a separate 7px span; this creates multiple competing typographic messages in a narrow viewport.
issues.observed: The first screen is visually dramatic but asks a mobile visitor to decode the brand, proposition, and next action through stacked translucent type over a busy image.
issues.expected: A premium mobile hero should retain one unequivocal reading sequence: brand, concise value proposition, then one primary action, with each layer legible at a glance over the image.
issues.location: Homepage hero, mobile viewport.
issues.recommendation: Recompose the mobile hero independently rather than scaling the desktop arrangement. Keep a compact wordmark, use a smaller high-contrast H1 on a controlled dark overlay or quieter image region, remove the duplicate/faint display treatment, and establish clear vertical separation before the CTA group.

issues.title: The primary property-discovery path lacks an immediate search or filtering entry point
issues.detail: The homepage leads with “Explore homes” and “Private search,” but the visible first screen does not let a buyer state their intent by area, price, bedrooms, property type, or new-build status. For an expensive, considered purchase in a multi-area market, that makes the route feel more editorial than task-oriented.
issues.evidence: The screenshot shows only two hero CTAs. The business requirements explicitly include filters and property discovery; the DOM exposes a properties route and listing links but no search/filter control on the homepage hero.
issues.observed: A buyer must make a broad navigation choice before narrowing an inventory set.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury property discovery combines the brand-led hero with an elegant, low-friction search entry that supports high-intent browsing without making the page feel like a commodity portal.
issues.location: Homepage hero and immediately below the fold.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a restrained search launcher or compact filter row at the hero transition: area, property type, price range, and bedrooms, plus an optional “off-market/private search” route. Preserve the editorial image while making the next step specific.

issues.title: The premium-advisory claim is not substantiated with visible proof or Marbella expertise
issues.detail: “Independent property advisory - Puerto Banus” establishes a positioning statement, but the page provides no visible advisor identity, transaction experience, market credentials, testimonial, partner recognition, or area-specific evidence in the supplied view. The scan likewise records zero trust signals.
issues.evidence: The hero screenshot contains the advisory descriptor but no credibility element. Objective scan: trustSignalCount is 0; bookingSignalCount is 0. The page contains 215 words, leaving limited room to establish differentiated expertise.
issues.observed: The brand asks visitors to trust a premium, buyer-led service on aesthetic presentation alone.
issues.expected: A credible premium real-estate platform should pair aspiration with a concise, verifiable reason to choose its advisory service, particularly before asking for an enquiry.
issues.location: Homepage hero transition, featured-property section, and private-search/contact route.
issues.recommendation: Add a tightly art-directed proof module: named local advisors with portrait, years/market specialization, a verifiable performance or client-service claim, and one concise client endorsement. Give private search a specific consultation or viewing-request expectation.

issues.title: Typography is elegant in intent but over-relies on very small, widely tracked utility text
issues.detail: The desktop navigation, contact label, eyebrow text, listing count, and action labels are rendered at very small sizes. This creates a fashion-editorial tone, but at several points the text is closer to decorative detail than comfortably scannable interface copy. Footer/secondary links are particularly small targets.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports 108 visible text elements flagged as tiny, including 7px FOR SALE, 8px discovery/listing labels, and many 10-11px navigation/action labels. It also identifies 17 undersized interactive targets, including area/navigation and footer links.
issues.observed: Important navigation and action language has reduced visual authority and risks looking delicate rather than deliberately premium.
issues.expected: Luxury interfaces can be restrained, but key navigation, labels, and actions should remain comfortably readable and have robust touch areas without depending on excessive tracking or tiny type.
issues.location: Global header, hero labels and CTAs, property-section utilities, and footer navigation.
issues.recommendation: Raise functional text to a more durable minimum size, reduce tracking where it weakens word shape, and retain the existing editorial scale only for nonessential micro-labels. Expand touch hit areas around text links, especially in the footer and saved-property controls.

issues.title: The proposition is polished but generic and underdeveloped for the market decision
issues.detail: “Marbella, chosen well.” and “Curated homes, new developments and a buyer-led search across Marbella and the Costa del Sol.” describe a desirable tone but do not explain the selection standard, target buyer, local advantage, or why a visitor should enquire here instead of with another luxury agency. The phrase “buyer-led search” is not made concrete.
issues.evidence: The screenshot contains the quoted hero messaging; the scan measures only 215 words of page content and records no trust signals. The content score is the lowest of the primary automated scores at 91.7, despite otherwise strong technical results.
issues.observed: The copy establishes mood but gives insufficient decision-supporting substance for a high-consideration property enquiry.
issues.expected: Reference-quality property copy should make the curation and advisory model tangible: relevant micro-markets, access to new/off-market opportunities where true, buyer needs served, and what happens after contact.
issues.location: Homepage hero, private-search CTA destination, and first editorial section.
issues.recommendation: Replace or support the abstract value line with concise, specific market language. Explain the selection criteria and buyer service in one or two sharp sentences, then reinforce it through area expertise and a clear enquiry outcome such as a tailored shortlist or advisor consultation.

issues.title: The hero presents two equal-weight actions without enough decision guidance
issues.detail: “Explore homes” is visually filled and “Private search” is outlined, but neither label explains the audience or outcome. A visitor with an immediate requirement may not know whether private search means a consultation, off-market access, a saved search, or a form.
issues.evidence: Both actions appear side by side in desktop and mobile screenshots. The scan finds three primary CTAs overall but no booking signal, so the advisory path is available without a visible commitment or response expectation.
issues.observed: The page offers choice but provides limited reassurance about what each route delivers.
issues.expected: The top conversion choice should be self-explanatory, with the high-touch route framed around a concrete premium benefit and a low-friction next step.
issues.location: Homepage hero CTA group.
issues.recommendation: Keep “Explore homes” as the inventory action and rename/support the secondary action with a tangible outcome, for example “Request a tailored shortlist” or “Talk to a Marbella advisor,” supported by a brief response-time or consultation cue where substantiated.

aiReview.summary: The homepage has a strong luxury-real-estate starting point: an authentic-looking villa image, restrained navigation, and a premium dark editorial mood. It is not yet reference-quality because the mobile hero loses hierarchy and legibility, property discovery is deferred behind a generic CTA, and the proposition lacks the proof and local specificity that justify a premium advisory position. The high automated results reflect a technically clean build and intact paths; the visual and commercial experience visible here needs more refinement.
strengths: The full-bleed dusk villa photograph is relevant, aspirational, and immediately signals Marbella luxury property rather than a generic brokerage template.
Desktop has a calm, spacious composition with limited competing UI, clear primary navigation, and a visually distinct primary action.
The required discovery and enquiry routes are present, internal paths resolve, the contact route is available, and no critical journey failure was detected.

The implementation supports the experience well: no horizontal overflow, zero measured layout shift, fast load metrics, labelled controls, image alt coverage, and no observed console or failed-network errors.
Property inventory is surfaced below the fold through named listings, while area and development routes provide sensible secondary discovery paths.

issues.detail: The cookie consent panel dominates the first visit and blocks both the hero CTA and a large portion of the restaurant imagery. On desktop it covers the lower-right hero area; on mobile it occupies nearly the full lower third of the viewport and obscures the continuation of the H1.
issues.evidence: Visible cookie panel overlays the hero in both supplied screenshots. The mobile panel is approximately 94% of viewport width and contains two large actions plus a policy link.
issues.expected: Consent should remain compliant while preserving immediate access to the reservation path and the core brand impression. A more compact bottom sheet, less intrusive modal, or delayed non-blocking presentation would keep the first action visible.
issues.location: Homepage first viewport, desktop and mobile
issues.observed: The visitor must process a large privacy panel before seeing the full headline or using the hero reservation CTA. The small 'CERRAR' text is less prominent than the consent actions.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the consent surface area, preserve the hero CTA above or beside it, and provide a clearly recognizable close/dismiss control with a compact mobile layout.
issues.title: Cookie consent obstructs the primary conversion moment

issues.detail: Reservation is present in the header and hero, but the hero's main message and CTA are not composed as a consistently accessible mobile-first reservation entry point. On mobile, the oversized headline drops below the visible area and is partly hidden by the consent panel.
issues.evidence: Desktop places 'RESERVAR MESA' low in the hero. Mobile shows the H1 breaking into two large lines beneath the header, with the lower line concealed by the overlay. The objective scan confirms multiple booking signals, but no form is present on the homepage.
issues.expected: A premium restaurant homepage should make the next reservation action obvious within the first mobile viewport, with a deliberate CTA position that survives overlays, headline wrapping, and common device heights.
issues.location: Homepage hero and mobile header
issues.observed: The reservation route exists, but the most persuasive first-screen sequence is visually interrupted and the mobile hero does not reliably expose the primary action.
issues.recommendation: Recompose the mobile hero around a visible reservation action, reserve a stable text region for the H1, and ensure consent or other utility UI cannot cover the conversion CTA.
issues.title: The mobile reservation path is not reliably visible

issues.detail: The mobile hero uses a very large editorial H1 that wraps awkwardly as 'Mar de' followed by 'verdad.' The second line is pushed into the consent overlay, making the intended typographic composition feel accidental rather than art-directed.
issues.evidence: The supplied mobile screenshot shows the first line of the H1 clearly and only the upper portion of the second line beneath the cookie panel. The desktop composition fits as one line, so the responsive type treatment is materially different.
issues.expected: Editorial display typography should retain intentional line breaks, readable hierarchy, and a complete composition at common mobile widths.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero headline
issues.observed: The headline is oversized for the available vertical space and its responsive wrap is not fully visible.
issues.recommendation: Define an intentional mobile line break or smaller display scale, constrain the text block, and test it with the consent state enabled at short mobile viewport heights.
issues.title: Hero typography loses control on mobile

issues.detail: The hero image establishes waterfront atmosphere but does not strongly deliver appetite or premium product value. It is primarily a table-setting scene, with no visible dish, ingredient, or service moment, and the heavy dark treatment reduces detail in the lower half.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots show chairs, glasses, linens, and waterfront context; no food is visible in the first viewport. The desktop image is substantially darkened beneath the navigation and hero copy, while the mobile crop is soft and heavily background-led.
issues.expected: The first image should communicate both the destination and the reason to dine there, using a sharper, appetizing focal subject with contrast tuned for legibility rather than simply applying a dark atmospheric treatment.
issues.location: Homepage hero imagery
issues.observed: The visual sells setting more effectively than cuisine, product quality, or a memorable signature experience.
issues.recommendation: Use a higher-detail image or art-directed image sequence that includes recognizable food or service while retaining the waterfront cue. Adjust the overlay locally behind text instead of darkening the whole image uniformly.
issues.title: Hero imagery under-delivers appetite and product value

issues.detail: Trust and practical visit information are not prominent in the first viewport despite being essential for a destination restaurant in Puerto Banus. The visible signals are mainly the location eyebrow and brand presentation; practical reassurance is deferred to navigation or later sections.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports only one trust signal. In the supplied first-viewport screenshots there is no visible review proof, award context, opening-hours cue, address detail, or reservation reassurance. The location is named, but the operational information needed before booking is not surfaced.
issues.expected: A premium restaurant should quickly answer why the guest should trust the venue and whether visiting is convenient, especially for visitors discovering it from Marbella or Puerto Banus.

aiReview.summary: La Bocana has a strong visual premise and a credible premium waterfront tone, but the first-visit experience is less conversion-ready than the automated scores suggest. The cookie panel interrupts the most important moment, mobile headline composition is not fully controlled, and the hero sells atmosphere more strongly than food, trust, or practical booking confidence. Refining the first viewport around a visible reservation action, sharper appetite-led imagery, and restrained trust/location information would move it closer to reference-quality premium restaurant execution.
strengths: The waterfront setting and Puerto Banus/Marbella location are immediately legible, giving the brand a credible destination cue.
The serif display typography, restrained navy/ivory palette, and generous composition support a premium editorial restaurant position.
Reservation is available through several visible routes, including the desktop header, mobile header, and hero CTA.
The navigation exposes the core discovery routes: menu, restaurant story, gallery, contact, reservation lookup, and booking.
The objective scan shows strong baseline quality: fast loading, zero layout shift, no horizontal overflow, valid internal links, accessible labels, and no console or network errors.

aiReview.summary: The captured experience is effectively a full-screen loading state on both desktop and mobile, not a usable premium real-estate website. A restrained burgundy palette may be appropriate for the positioning, but no brand, property inventory, imagery, navigation, expertise, or enquiry path becomes visible. The objective scan confirms that the rendered DOM contains only 3 words, 6 visible elements, one interactive target, no H1, no images, no navigation links, no form, no CTA, and no trust signals. Strong technical measurements cannot compensate for the absence of the actual business experience.
strengths: The burgundy and copper palette has the potential to support an elegant, premium identity.
The loading state is visually consistent across desktop and mobile, with no measured horizontal overflow or layout shift.
The page responds successfully with no failed requests or console errors, and baseline accessibility checks pass for the very limited rendered interface.
